processing: Withered, rolled, oxidised and fired in the orthodox Darjeeling way; spring lots are oxidised lightly, summer lots further. The estate says it still runs old machinery to keep a traditional style.
harvest_season: The estate singles out its first and second flushes, picked from March to June, as the most concentrated. As elsewhere in Darjeeling, monsoon and autumn pickings follow.
appearance_dry: As with other China-bush Darjeelings, small wiry leaf, olive and silver in spring lots and darker brown with golden tips in summer lots.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to light amber in first flush, deeper amber-copper in second flush.
appearance_wet: Small, supple leaves, green with reddish edges in spring and more evenly coppery in summer.
taste_profile: The garden is known for China-character and muscatel teas: expect, as is typical of the type, a floral spring cup and a riper, grape-skin summer cup with a dry finish.

brewing.notes: Western-style. Use cooler water, around 85°C, for first flush, and go near the boil for second flush.

vintage_note: Sold by year and flush, with lot numbers and grades such as SFTGFOP1 on estate-named lots. First flush lots from a given spring are usually drunk within about a year; second flush holds a little longer. Check the year and the flush, as both change the cup completely.
description:
Orange Valley is a Darjeeling garden that used to go by the name Bloomfield, and you will still meet both names. It sits on a north-east-facing mountainside near Darjeeling town, and takes its current name, by one account, from the orange trees around the property.

The owners describe an unusually wide altitude spread, 3,500 to 6,000 feet, on gentle slopes, and they say they keep old machines running to hold on to a traditional style. Orthodox Darjeeling processing does the rest: light oxidation in spring, more in summer.

Its reputation rests on China-character and muscatel teas. As with other Darjeelings, the first flush should be floral and brisk and the second rounder and fruitier. Steep spring lots cooler than you would a normal black tea, or they turn sharp.

The garden carries organic and Fair Trade certifications among others, so look for those marks along with the year and flush. Lots named Orange Valley and lots named Bloomfield can both turn up, so check the seller's description if the name matters to you.
history:
The garden was planted by the British, though no founding year is firmly documented. It ran as Bloomfield Tea Garden until ownership moved from the Bloomfield Tea Company to Orange Valley Tea Limited, when it took its present name.

It now belongs to the Bagaria Group. Published figures for its altitude differ somewhat, with 5,000 to 6,000 feet given as well as the owners' wider range.
